question: Why does the pipeline generate audio first and time visuals to the measured audio (the timing block), and how do parallel scene-builders render standalone HyperFrames scenes before stitching?
answer_summary: The pipeline voices the script first and measures the real audio, because TTS length cannot be predicted from word counts (numbers made a draft run 40% long). Scene-builders then key every on-screen change to the measured timing, one standalone HyperFrames project per scene in parallel, so a broken scene can be fixed and re-rendered alone before assemble.py stitches the renders.

facts.claim: The repository states audio-first as a key design rule: visuals are timed to the measured voiceover, never the reverse.
facts.source_title: capstone-video-agent README, section 3 Key design rules
facts.excerpt: **Audio first.** Visuals are timed to the measured voiceover, never the reverse.

facts.claim: Audio is measured rather than estimated because TTS reads numbers in full, making number-heavy scripts run about 25% longer than word counts suggest; the pipeline measures real audio and trims before fact-checking.
facts.source_title: capstone-video-agent README, section 3 Key design rules
facts.excerpt: a number-heavy script runs ~25% longer than a word count suggests. The pipeline measures real audio and trims before fact-checking.

facts.claim: In the first end-to-end run, the measured voiceover was 83.8 s against a 60 s target (+40%), and a trim pass brought the final video to 56.0 s.
facts.source_title: Step 2 Results: Agent Pipeline, First 60-Second Run

facts.claim: The scene-builder takes the already-measured timing from scenes.json, copies it into a TIMING block, and keys every on-screen change to the line start rather than typing times by hand.
facts.excerpt: Copy `timing` into the TIMING block exactly. Key **every** on-screen change to `at(line_id)`; never type a time by hand.

facts.claim: The orchestrator launches one scene-builder per scene in a single message so they run in parallel, then assemble.py checks, renders each scene to renders/<id>.mp4 and stitches them into the final MP4.
facts.excerpt: Launch one **scene-builder** subagent per scene, **all in the same message**

facts.claim: Each scene is a standalone HyperFrames project so a broken scene can be fixed and re-rendered alone; the repair loop allows one attempt per scene via assemble.py --only.
facts.source_title: capstone-video-agent README, section 3 Key design rules
facts.excerpt: **One scene = one standalone HyperFrames project**, so a broken scene is fixed and re-rendered alone.

conflicts: README says number-heavy scripts run ~25% longer than word counts suggest; the first run's draft was +40% over target (83.8 s vs 60 s). These are different measures (typical vs one run), not a true contradiction.
gaps: Exact fields of the timing block (e.g. scene_duration_s, vo_offset_s, audio_duration_s) are only named in scene-builder.md; no sample filled scenes.json was read.
No stated rationale for parallel scene building beyond the run-time note that research and scene building dominate time at 7 minutes (docs/step2-results.md).
